facts.fact_text: The case concerns the respondent State's alleged failure to protect the applicants, all of whom are members of the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex (LGBTI) community, from homophobic acts of violence by private individuals.
Some applicants complained that they had been apprehended and detained unlawfully during peaceful demonstrations in support of LGBTI people.
On 17 May 2012 Mr Romanov took part in the 'Rainbow flash mob' event in St Petersburg.
The 'Rainbow flash mob' event in St Petersburg on 17 May 2012 had been authorised by the local authorities.
The 'Rainbow flash mob' event in St Petersburg on 17 May 2012 marked the International Day Against Homophobia and Transphobia.
On 11 January 2013 Mr Lebedev and Mr Nasonov notified the authorities in Voronezh of their intent to hold a demonstration involving about fifty participants on 20 January 2013.
The planned demonstration on 20 January 2013 in Voronezh was against the enactment of the law banning 'propaganda of non-traditional sexual relations'.
The authorities in Voronezh authorised the demonstration planned for 20 January 2013.

On 29 June 2013 Mr Starov, Ms Pitenova, Mr Fedorov and Mr Prokopenko took part in a demonstration involving about eighty participants in St Petersburg aimed at drawing attention to violations of the rights of LGBTI people in Russia.
The local authorities had been notified in advance of the demonstration of 29 June 2013 in St Petersburg.
On 12 October 2013 Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina intended to take part in a demonstration in St Petersburg to mark Coming Out Day.
On 3 November 2013 Mr Chechetkin attended the 'Rainbow Tea Social', a weekly event held to support LGBTI people, at an HIV prevention centre in St Petersburg.
The police did not intervene when counter-demonstrators started insulting the participants in the 'Rainbow flash mob' event on 17 May 2012.
During the 'Rainbow flash mob' event on 17 May 2012, one of the counter-demonstrators, Mr L., fired five times towards Mr Romanov with a spray gun.
On 20 January 2013 more than one hundred counter-demonstrators came to the site of the LGBTI demonstration in Voronezh, where six participants were present.

On 20 January 2013 counter-demonstrators at the site of the LGBTI demonstration in Voronezh unfolded banners with homophobic slogans and called for violence against the participants in the demonstration.
On 20 January 2013 counter-demonstrators threw snowballs and paint balloons at the participants in the LGBTI demonstration in Voronezh and tore up the participants' posters.
At around 2 p.m. on 20 January 2013 some of the counter-demonstrators beat Mr Lebedev and Mr Nasonov at the site of the LGBTI demonstration in Voronezh.
About forty police officers were present at the site of the LGBTI demonstration in Voronezh on 20 January 2013 but did not intervene.
All the participants in the LGBTI demonstration in Voronezh on 20 January 2013 had to stop the demonstration and leave.
Counter-demonstrators at the demonstration of 29 June 2013 in St Petersburg shouted homophobic slogans, called for violence against the participants and threw stones and smoke bombs at them.
At around 3 p.m. on 29 June 2013 one of the counter-demonstrators ran up to Mr Prokopenko and punched him in the face and hands.
The police present at the scene of the demonstration of 29 June 2013 in St Petersburg did not intervene when counter-demonstrators attacked the participants.
While Mr Starov, Ms Pitenova and Mr Fedorov were walking away from the demonstration of 29 June 2013 in St Petersburg, about thirty counter-demonstrators ran up to them and started beating them.

Counter-demonstrators at the site of the demonstration of 12 October 2013 in St Petersburg shouted homophobic slogans, pushed Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina and prevented them from proceeding to the venue.

The police did not intervene when counter-demonstrators pushed Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina and prevented them from proceeding to the venue of the demonstration of 12 October 2013 in St Petersburg.

At 1.55 p.m. on 12 October 2013, five minutes before the demonstration started, the police began apprehending the participants, including Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina, on the grounds that they had used foul language.
At 2.30 p.m. on 12 October 2013 the police escorted Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina to a police station.

Administrative-offence reports were drawn up against Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina under Article 20.1 § 1 ('petty hooliganism' – мелкое хулиганство) of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation following their apprehension on 12 October 2013.
Mr Fedorov and Ms Levina complained that they had been apprehended and detained unlawfully, before the start of the authorised demonstration of 12 October 2013 in St Petersburg.

Mr Prokopenko brought a civil action seeking compensation for non-pecuniary damage caused by his being unlawfully apprehended and detained before the start of the authorised demonstration of 12 October 2013 in St Petersburg.

At around 7.15 p.m. on 3 November 2013 two young men in hoods armed with a baseball bat and an air gun entered the HIV prevention centre in St Petersburg where the 'Rainbow Tea Social' event was being held.
As soon as Mr Chechetkin turned his head in the direction of the intruders, one of them shot him in the left eye with an air gun.
One of the attackers shouted 'where are you going, faggot?' at Mr Chechetkin and then approached him and hit him in the shoulder and leg with a baseball bat.

Administrative-offence reports were drawn up against Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina under Article 20.1 § 1 ('petty hooliganism' – мелкое хулиганство) of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation following their apprehension on 12 October 2013.

Article 63 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides a list of aggravated circumstances of a crime, which includes committing a crime on the grounds of political, ideological, racial, national, or religious hatred, or on the grounds of hostility or hatred towards any social group.

Article 111 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the intentional infliction of severe harm to a person's health, the endangering of their life, or the causing of harm resulting in the loss of sight, speech, hearing or any organ or the loss of its functions, termination of a pregnancy, mental disorder, drug addiction or substance abuse, or harm resulting in the irreparable disfigurement of the face or causing a significant and persistent loss of general working capacity by at least one third or a complete loss of professional working capacity, shall be punishable by imprisonment for a term of up to eight years.

Article 111 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the same acts as in Article 111 § 1, if committed against a person or their close relatives in connection with the performance of official duties, against a minor or person in a helpless state, in a generally dangerous manner, for hire, for disorderly motives, on the grounds of political, ideological, racial, national or religious hatred or enmity or on the grounds of hostility or hatred towards any social group, or for the purpose of using the organs or tissues of the victim, shall be punishable by imprisonment for a term of up to ten years, with or without a restriction of liberty for a term of up to two years.

Article 111 § 3 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the acts provided for in the first or second part of Article 111, if committed by a group of persons, a group of persons upon prior conspiracy or an organised group, or against two or more persons, shall be punishable by imprisonment for a term of up to twelve years, with or without a restriction of liberty for a term of up to two years.

Article 116 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the infliction of beatings or other violent actions causing physical pain but not resulting in the consequences specified in Article 115 of the Criminal Code shall be punishable by a fine of up to RUB 40,000, or by the seizure of the convicted person's wages or other income for a period of up to three months, or by community service for a period of up to 360 hours, or by corrective labour for a period of up to six months or by imprisonment for a term of up to three months.

Article 116 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the same acts as in Article 116 § 1, if committed for disorderly motives or on grounds of political, ideological, racial, national or religious hatred or enmity or on grounds of hostility or hatred towards any social group, shall be punishable by community service for a period of up to 360 hours, or by corrective labour for a period of up to one year, or by restriction of liberty for a period of up to two years, or by compulsory labour for a period of up to two years, or by imprisonment for a term of up to six months or by deprivation of liberty for a period of up to two years.

Article 282 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that actions aimed at inciting hatred or enmity and humiliating the dignity of an individual or a group of individuals on the grounds of gender, race, ethnic origin, language, background, religious beliefs or membership of a social group, committed publicly or in the mass media, shall be punishable by a fine of from RUB 100,000 to RUB 300,000 or an amount equivalent to the convicted person's wages or other income for a period of from one to two years, or by the withdrawal of the right to hold certain posts or carry out certain activities for a period of up to three years, or by community service for a period of up to 360 hours, or by corrective labour for a period of up to one year, or by compulsory labour for a period of up to two years or by deprivation of liberty of up to two years.

Article 282 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the same actions as in Article 282 § 1, if committed with the use of violence or the threat of its use, by a person using his or her official position, or by an organised group, are punishable by a fine of RUB 100,000 to RUB 500,000 or an amount equivalent to the convicted person's wages or other income for a period of from one to three years, or by the withdrawal of the right to hold certain posts or carry out certain activities for a period of up to five years, or by community service for a period of up to 480 hours, or by corrective labour for a period of from one to two years, or by compulsory labour for a period of up to five years or by deprivation of liberty of up to five years.
Until 3 July 2016 any form of 'battery' had constituted a criminal offence under Article 116 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.

On 3 July 2016 the 'non-aggravated' form of battery was decriminalised and reclassified as an administrative offence under Article 6.1.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation.

Article 6.1.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provides that the infliction of beatings or the commission of other violent actions that cause physical pain but do not result in the consequences specified in Article 115 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation shall, as long as these acts do not constitute a criminal offense, entail the imposition of an administrative fine of from RUB 5,000 to RUB 30,000, or administrative detention for a period of from ten to fifteen days or community service for a period of from sixty to 120 hours.

The local authorities deployed 165 police officers to maintain public order at the site of the demonstration of 29 June 2013 in St Petersburg.
About 500 police officers were deployed to ensure public order during the demonstration of 12 October 2013 in St Petersburg.

On 17 July 2013 Mr Romanov requested the investigator to explore alleged motives of hate against LGBTI people in the case concerning the attack on him on 17 May 2012.
By a decision of 18 July 2012, the investigator dismissed Mr Romanov's request to explore hate motives against LGBTI people for 'lack of any evidence of hate motives'.

In the decision of 18 July 2012, the investigator indicated that Mr L. had not insulted anyone, had come to the event by accident, and that his actions had been motivated by the blasphemous words on the balloon.
On 18 December 2013 the State Duma of the Russian Federation amnestied Mr L.
On 12 February 2014 the St Petersburg City Court discontinued the case against Mr L. in accordance with the Amnesty Act.

On 19 January 2013 Mr Lebedev and Mr Nasonov asked the police to open a criminal case under Article 119 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation and to grant them protection, enclosing printouts of the threatening messages.

The organisers of the demonstration planned for 20 January 2013 in Voronezh notified the police of a counter-demonstration which was to take place at the same venue with the aim of obstructing the event.
On 30 January 2013 the police refused Mr Nasonov's application to have a criminal investigation opened.

Mr Z. was released from the obligation to serve his sentence on the grounds that the limitation period had expired.
The police suspended the criminal proceedings against other attackers of Mr Lebedev and Mr Nasonov owing to the impossibility of identifying the suspects.

Mr Starov, Ms Pitenova, Mr Fedorov and Mr Prokopenko sought to have a criminal investigation opened into the homophobic attacks on them on 29 June 2013.
The police questioned some of the participants who had been assaulted during the demonstration of 29 June 2013 but never identified the perpetrators.

Between July 2013 and December 2015 the police repeatedly refused to open a criminal investigation into battery committed for hate motives under Article 116 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation in relation to the attacks of 29 June 2013, citing a 'hostile attitude of people of heterosexual orientation towards members of the LGBTI community'.

The prosecutor quashed the police's repeated decisions not to open a criminal investigation into the attacks of 29 June 2013 each time and ordered additional inquiries, emphasising the need to identify and question eyewitnesses of the attacks on the applicants.

Following the last decision by the police on 23 December 2015 not to initiate a criminal investigation into the attacks of 29 June 2013, the police did not carry out the measures ordered by the prosecutor.

On 4 November 2013, at the request of Ms P., the police opened a criminal case in respect of the attack on Mr Chechetkin at the HIV prevention centre.
All persons questioned by the police between November 2013 and February 2014 about the attack of 3 November 2013 alleged that the attack had been motivated by hatred against LGBTI people.

On 24 December 2013 the investigator refused an application by Mr Chechetkin's lawyer for the perpetrators' actions to be classified under Article 111 § 3 (a) and (b) of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation as actions committed by a group of persons for motives of hatred or enmity towards LGBTI people.
On 16 July 2014 the investigator suspended the investigation into the attack on Mr Chechetkin on the grounds that the attackers could not be identified.
The investigators suspended and resumed the investigation into the attack on Mr Chechetkin multiple times, most recently on 7 October 2017, without achieving any tangible results.

On 23 October 2017 the police refused to institute criminal proceedings in relation to the attack on Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin, stating that 'the attack had amounted to an administrative offence under Article 6.1.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation' ('battery').
No criminal investigation was ever instituted in relation to the attack on Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin on 14 October 2017.
On 14 October 2019 the police discontinued the administrative proceedings in relation to the attack on Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin on the grounds that the limitation period had expired.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe provides that member states should ensure effective, prompt and impartial investigations into alleged cases of crimes and other incidents where the sexual orientation or gender identity of the victim is reasonably suspected to have constituted a motive for the perpetrator.

The European Commission against Racism and Intolerance noted in its report CRI(2019)2 that the Constitutional Court of the Russian Federation's 2014 interpretation that 'any social group' can apply to a group of individuals with a specific sexual orientation does not seem to be reflected in regular court practice.

The European Commission against Racism and Intolerance noted in its report CRI(2019)2 that the United Nations expressed concern about the fact that Article 63 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation on aggravating circumstances does not appear to have ever been applied to cases involving violence against LGBTI persons, in spite of a high number of such incidents.

In its concluding observations on the seventh periodic report of the Russian Federation of 28 April 2015 (CCPR/C/RUS/7), the United Nations Human Rights Committee expressed concern that Article 63 § 1 (e) of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation, recognising as aggravated circumstances the commission of an offence for reasons of 'hatred or enmity' or 'hate or hostility towards a given social group', does not appear to have ever been applied to cases involving violence against LGBTI individuals.

In its concluding observations CCPR/C/RUS/7, the United Nations Human Rights Committee stated that the Russian Federation should take all the steps necessary to ensure the investigation, prosecution and punishment of any act of violence motivated by the victim's sexual orientation or gender identity and apply the provisions of Article 63 § 1 (e) of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation to such acts.
